source.versionTitle: Adapa — best-effort reconstruction from named scholarly editions
source.verificationStatus: best-effort reconstruction from named scholarship (Knudtzon 1915 PD for Fragment A; Picchioni 1981; Lambert in studies; Izre'el 2001 LSU 10 the modern critical edition; Foster Before the Muses 3rd ed 2005). Verification pending against the Izre'el 2001 primary critical edition. Transliteration may contain sign-value reconstruction errors at the per-line level; sense-of-line is well-attested across editions and should match downstream English faithfully.
source.license: Transliteration is best-effort reconstruction from cited scholarly editions; all WoH English original to this project.
source.fetchedFrom: scholarly editions (not openly digitized — see verificationStatus)
citations: Knudtzon, J. A., Die el-Amarna-Tafeln (Leipzig 1907-1915), text 356 (PD; Fragment A primary source).
Picchioni, S. A., Il poemetto di Adapa (Budapest 1981).
Izre'el, S., Adapa and the South Wind: Language Has the Power of Life and Death (Mesopotamian Civilizations 10, Winona Lake 2001) — the modern critical edition and standard scholarly reference.
Foster, B. R., Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature, 3rd ed. (Bethesda 2005), pp. 525-530 — the accessible English translation.
Lambert, W. G., 'A late Assyrian catalogue of literary and scholarly texts,' in Festschrift Jacobsen (1976) — for Fragment D catchline.
Heidel, A., The Babylonian Genesis (Chicago 1942), pp. 147-153 — earlier widely-cited English translation (older editions may be partially PD).
source.fragmentationNote: Adapa is preserved in 4 fragments from different periods and excavation sites. Fragment A (Old Babylonian / Middle Babylonian, found at Tell el-Amarna as letter EA 356) — ~13 lines, Adapa's creation by Ea. Fragment B (Neo-Assyrian, K.8214+ from Nineveh) — ~75 lines, the main narrative. Fragments C and D (Late Babylonian) — small, ~10-15 lines combined; D preserves the catchline. Total ~100 lines preserved; lacunae between fragments cannot be reliably estimated.

segments.label: Fragment A — Amarna EA 356 (Old Babylonian / Middle Babylonian, found at Tell el-Amarna)

notes: Opening: Ea's address. The Akkadian text references Adapa's standing before Anu. Knudtzon 1915 reads ina pān; restored.
'…the whole of heaven, knowing fear.' Ea presents Adapa as a paradigm of the god-fearing wise human.
'The son of Ea brought (with him) the speech of his bitterness…' — the obscure description of Adapa's mouth/speech. Multiple readings in scholarship.
Of uncertain meaning; readings vary. Izre'el 2001 and Foster 2005 differ.
'He (= Ea) set Adapa as the god-fearing one.' Adapa appointed as the paradigm-sage.
'To all the lands, his name (renown).' Adapa's name spreads through the lands.
'He (= Ea) made/gave him the heart of the diadem(?) of heaven.' The 'heart of the diadem' or 'crown of heaven' is a metaphor for Ea's gift of wisdom.
'He made him great; the (council of) gods praised(?).' Adapa is exalted among the gods.
'With the gods…' (broken). Adapa stands among the gods despite being human.

lines.translit: ne-me-qa id-din-šu napišta dāriti ul id-din-šu
notes: **MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'He gave him wisdom (*nēmequ*) — eternal life (*napištu dārītu*) he did not give him.' THE FOUNDATIONAL CRUX of the Adapa story: Ea grants Adapa wisdom but withholds immortality. The Adapa-as-paradigm-sage but mortal-by-design framework. Cross-corpus the Hebrew Gen 3:22 tree-of-life motif. Verification pending against Izre'el's exact reading.
'In those days … the son of Ea daily(?)' — narrative-temporal frame for the Eridu service.

lines.translit: ašar (d)Ea ina qereb Eridu(KI) ina ramāni-šu(?) ibšû
notes: 'Where Ea dwelt in the midst of Eridu by his own (creative power).' Eridu is Ea's cosmographic seat (cross-corpus the abzu/apsû concept).

'… Adapa [king(?) of the black-headed people].' The closing line of Fragment A, broken; Adapa's epithet possibly as ruler/leader of humankind. *ṣalmāt qaqqadi* 'black-headed people' is the Akkadian self-designation for humanity (cross-corpus the Sumerian *saĝ-gig-ga* central entry from the Flood Story; bidirectional cross-corpus sibling-cluster candidate).

segments.label: Fragment B — K.8214+ Neo-Assyrian Nineveh (the main narrative)

preceding_lacuna.text: Lacuna of unknown size between Fragments A and B; Fragment B is a Neo-Assyrian Nineveh tablet preserving the main narrative.

i18n.en: [Lacuna of unknown size between Fragments A and B. Fragment B preserves the main Neo-Assyrian narrative as recovered from the Kuyunjik library at Nineveh.]

notes: '…Adapa, son of Eridu.' The fragment opens with Adapa identified as the wise-man of Eridu.

lines.translit: ina qereb Eridu(KI) (d)Ea ina mayyāli-šu i-nu-uš-šu
notes: 'In the midst of Eridu, Ea woke him on his bed.' / 'Ea roused him from his couch.' Ea-as-master-of-Adapa relationship.
'Daily(?) in Eridu he [drew(?)] the pure waters.' Adapa's role as Ea's servant — drawing the pure water for the cult.
'He went up; he rode in his boat.' Adapa's daily routine of going out to fish for Ea's temple.

lines.translit: ina ūmi šuāti ana tâmti dalti(?) ša bāb Eridu(KI) išteni
notes: 'On that day to the sea-gate of Eridu he set out alone.' The fishing-expedition that triggers the South Wind incident.

lines.translit: [X X] elippa-šu nāru ina(?) mê i-šat-tu
notes: '… his boat the wave / current drove on the waters.' / 'The wave bore his boat upon the waters.' Adapa is on the sea fishing.

lines.translit: ina libbi tâmti ša rapaš-tum (d)Šūtu(IM.U18.LU) ina pâ-ni-šu it-bi
notes: 'In the midst of the broad sea, the South Wind (*Šūtu* / *IM.U18.LU*) rose against him.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Šūtu* (the South Wind) — divinized wind. Cross-corpus the Akkadian wind-vocabulary; cross-corpus Hebrew *ruach* and the four cardinal winds tradition.

lines.translit: elippa-šu uṭebbi-šu Adapa ana bīt nūni iṭṭebi-šu
notes: '(The South Wind) sank his boat; Adapa was thrust into the fish's house (= drowned/submerged).' The capsizing event. *bīt nūni* 'house of the fish' as a poetic for the depths.
'O South Wind, [I will break(?)] — South Wind, I shall see your wing (lit. demon-form)!' Adapa's anger; he speaks against the South Wind.

**MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'May I break your wing (*kappī-ki*)!' — by the word of his mouth. The famous Adapa-breaks-the-South-Wind's-wing curse. **The wind-breaking by speech-act**: Izre'el 2001's subtitle is *Language Has the Power of Life and Death* — this is the central thesis-line. The speech-act efficacy: Adapa's spoken word breaks an immortal wind's wing. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE on the speech-act-efficacy motif; cross-corpus Hebrew creation-by-speech in Gen 1 (*va-yomer Elohim*); cross-corpus John 1:1 (*ho logos*).

lines.translit: ki-i ša ina pī-šu iqbû kapp(i) Šūti is-sa-bir
notes: 'As he spoke with his mouth, the wing of the South Wind broke (passive).' The speech-act takes effect.

lines.translit: sebet ūmī Šūtu ana māti ul iziq
notes: **MANDATORY**: 'For seven days the South Wind did not blow upon the land.' The cosmic-disturbance from Adapa's curse. Cross-corpus the seven-day flood-storm (Flood Story Segment D), the seven-day mourning (Genesis 50, etc.) — the seven-day cosmic-marker pattern.
'Anu spoke a word to his vizier Ilabrat.' Anu the sky-god takes notice; Ilabrat (Ninšubur in Sumerian, Ea's-counterpart-as-Anu's-vizier) reports.

lines.translit: mīnâ Šūtu ūmišamma ana māti ul iziq
notes: 'Why has the South Wind not blown upon the land for (these) days?'
'Ilabrat the vizier answered him.'

lines.translit: bēlī Adapa māru ša Ea kappi Šūti iš-bir
notes: 'My lord, Adapa son of Ea has broken the wing of the South Wind.'
'… Anu heard, and his anger arose.' Anu summons Adapa to heaven.

lines.translit: lišēriba-šu lišā ana mahar-ya — qiba ana Adapa
notes: 'Let him bring him up, let him come into my presence! Speak to Adapa!' Anu's command for the ascent.

lines.translit: (d)Ea apkal Eridu(KI) idī šipra ša šamê
notes: 'Ea, the sage of Eridu, knew the work of heaven.' Ea anticipates the summons; he prepares Adapa.

lines.translit: Adapa qarrāda iddi-šu-ma qarrāda mali kāspa idki-šu
notes: 'He set Adapa in dishevelled (mourning) hair; he made him wear mourning-garments.' Ea instructs Adapa to appear as a mourner before Anu's heavenly court.
'To Adapa Ea set words (= gave instructions).' The famous Ea-instruction speech follows.

lines.translit: Adapa ana mahar (d)Anu šarri ana šamê tellû
notes: 'Adapa, you are about to ascend to heaven, to the presence of Anu the king.'

lines.translit: ina kâdi ša bāb šamê (d)Dumuzi u (d)Gizzida izzazzū
notes: 'At the threshold of heaven's gate Dumuzi and Gizzida stand watch.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: Dumuzi and Gizzida as the gate-keeping deities of heaven; cross-corpus the dying-and-rising god motif (Dumuzi = Tammuz, cf. Ezek 8:14).

lines.translit: kī immarū-ka — ʾalka? ammīni? aššum manni?
notes: 'When they see you, they will ask — Where are you (going)? Why? For whose sake?'
'Place a sweet word before them.' Ea instructs Adapa to win their favor with kind words.

lines.translit: ašalūki — ana ilī šina ša ina mātīni iḫalliqū
notes: 'I will go ask — for the two gods who have disappeared from our land.' Adapa is to claim he mourns Dumuzi and Gizzida (the dying-vegetation-deities who have vanished from earth in the dry season). This flatters them: they receive cult-recognition.

lines.translit: kī iqabbi-ka — mannu šunu? Adapa — Dumuzi u Gizzida
notes: 'When they ask — who are they? Adapa: Dumuzi and Gizzida (themselves)!' Adapa's flattery confesses that the missing-vegetation-gods he mourns are the very gods now before him.

lines.translit: iḫdū-ma ana mahar Anu damiqta iqabbū-ka
notes: 'They will rejoice; and before Anu they will speak good (of you).' The gate-keepers will intercede for Adapa.
'Anu will (then) show you his favorable face.' The audience-pacification trick is set.

lines.translit: ina mahar Anu izziz-ma akala ša mūti ukallū-ka — ul takkala
notes: **MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'When you stand before Anu, they will offer you the bread of death — do not eat (it).' THE FAMOUS EA-DECEPTION (or 'Ea's misadvice' — debated in scholarship): Ea tells Adapa that the food Anu will offer is *akāl mūti* 'food of death'. Whether Ea deceives Adapa or is himself deceived is the central interpretive crux of the entire poem. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE — the crux of the lost-immortality narrative. Cross-corpus Gen 3:22 (the tree-of-life kept from humanity); Gen 2:17 (eat-and-die warning); the Eve-and-fruit forbidden-food motif.
'They will offer you the water of death — do not drink (it).' Parallel to v30 — the second forbidden-substance warning.
'They will offer you a garment — put it on.' Garment OK (no death-curse on the garment, per Ea's instruction).
'They will offer you oil — anoint yourself.' Oil OK as well — the contrast with food/water sharpens the suspicion that Ea's warning about food/water is deliberate.

lines.translit: ṭēmu ša aqbâ-kum la teggâ — amāt ša aqbâ-kum ukāl
notes: 'The instruction I have given you, do not transgress — the word I have given you, hold (fast).' Ea closes his speech with the binding-of-Adapa to obedience.

lines.translit: tâbi(?) ša Eridu Adapa illika ana šamê i-ti-li
notes: 'The good(/wise) one of Eridu, Adapa, went; he ascended to heaven.' Adapa's ascent.

lines.translit: ina kâdi ša bāb Anu Dumuzi u Gizzida i-ta-tu-šú
notes: 'At the threshold of Anu's gate, Dumuzi and Gizzida noticed him.' The gate-keepers encounter Adapa as Ea predicted.

lines.translit: Adapa ammīni qarrāda u kāspu tu-na-as-saḫ?
notes: 'Adapa, why have you put on dishevelled hair and mourning-garment?'

lines.translit: ina mātīni ilāni šina iḫliqū-ma ana-ku qarrāda lā nasḫāku
notes: 'In our land two gods have disappeared, therefore I am (dressed) in mourning-hair.' (The flattering ambiguity Ea coached: Adapa speaks of Dumuzi and Gizzida who 'disappear' annually from the land — the listeners now revealed as those very gods.)

lines.translit: mannu šunu ilāni šina? — Dumuzi u Gizzida
notes: 'Who are these two gods? — Dumuzi and Gizzida.' The flattery is delivered.
'They (Dumuzi and Gizzida) looked at one another; they smiled (?).' The gate-keepers are flattered.

lines.translit: ana mahar Anu i-mu-uš-šu-ma damiqta iqabbū
notes: 'Before Anu they came forward and spoke a good word (for Adapa).'
'Anu turned his favorable face (to Adapa).'
'Adapa, why have you broken the wing of the South Wind?'

lines.translit: bēlī ina libbi tâmti ša rapaš-tum ana bīt bēlī-ya nūni a-ṣa-id
notes: 'My lord — in the midst of the broad sea, for my lord's house I was netting fish.'
'The sea (rose) like a sanctuary-pavilion (a high vault).' Description of the storm.
'The South Wind blew and capsized my boat.'

lines.translit: ana bīt nūni it-ti-bi-(an)-ni — ina libbati-ya Šūta luš-bi-ir
notes: 'It thrust me into the fish-house (of the deep). In my anger I (cursed/spoke against) the South Wind so as to break (her wing).'
'Anu pondered (this) in his heart.'

lines.translit: Dumuzi u Gizzida ana Anu i-ma-an-nu-ma
notes: 'Dumuzi and Gizzida recounted (his case) to Anu.'

lines.translit: Anu lib-ba-šu i-pa-šaḫ — ana mīna Ea pālīḫa ana mār ša awīluti tu-lap-pi-it?
notes: **MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'Anu's heart was appeased. (He said:) Why did Ea reveal (the secrets) of heaven and earth to a human being? — and (give) him a strong heart?' The CENTRAL THEODICY-CRUX: Anu observes that Ea has given a HUMAN being divine wisdom, and (in some readings) is dismayed by this divine-secret-leak. Cross-corpus Gen 3:22 'the human has become like one of us, knowing good and evil' — the divine-recognition-of-stolen-divinity moment. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: šuāti mīnâ niqâb-šu? — akāl balāṭi liblū-šu — likul
notes: **MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'For him, what shall we (now) decree? — Let them bring him **food of life** (*akāl balāṭi*) — let him eat!' The IRONIC REVERSAL: what Ea called *akāl mūti* 'food of death' is in fact *akāl balāṭi* 'food of LIFE.' Either (a) Ea deceived Adapa to prevent humanity from gaining immortality (the deception-reading); (b) Ea genuinely didn't know (the misadvice-reading); (c) Anu's offer was conditional on Adapa's right-relating to it. The CRUX OF THE ENTIRE POEM. Cross-corpus the Hebrew tree-of-life and the 'will become like the gods' Gen 3:5-6+22 narrative; cross-corpus John 6:48-58 'I am the bread of life' (a Christian-soteriological echo that must be DISAVOWED — not pre-resolve to Christian-typology).

**MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'Let them bring him **water of life** (*mê balāṭi*) — let him drink!' Parallel to v51 — the divine-immortality water. Cross-corpus John 4:10-14 the living-water Christian-soteriological echo (DISAVOW); cross-corpus Rev 22:1 the river of life from the throne of God; cross-corpus Hebrew Gen 2:10 the four rivers of Eden.
'Let them bring him garment — let him put (it) on.' (The non-deadly accompaniment.)
'Let them bring him oil — let him anoint himself.' (The non-deadly accompaniment.)

lines.translit: akāl balāṭi ana mahri-šu ub-lu-ma — Adapa ul ikkal
notes: **MANDATORY MAJOR**: 'They brought the food of life before him — but Adapa did not eat.' The MOMENT of the lost-immortality. Adapa, obeying Ea's coached warning, refuses what would have given him eternal life. Cross-corpus Gen 3:6 (Eve eats and gains god-knowledge but loses Eden); Gen 3:22 (the tree-of-life kept from humanity by divine action). The INVERSE-PARALLEL: in Adapa, humanity refuses the divine food and loses immortality; in Genesis, humanity eats the divine food and loses immortality. Same cosmic-result via opposite human-action.

lines.translit: mê balāṭi ana mahri-šu ub-lu-ma — ul išatti
notes: 'They brought the water of life before him — but he did not drink.' Parallel to v55.

lines.translit: lubuš ub-lu-ma — il-tab-aš — šamna ub-lu-ma — ip-ta-as-sa-as
notes: 'They brought the garment — he put it on. They brought the oil — he anointed himself.' Adapa accepts the non-deadly gifts.

**MANDATORY**: 'Anu looked at him, and laughed (*īṣiḫ*).' Anu's reaction to Adapa's refusal: laughter (in some readings: incredulous; in others: amused at Ea's craftiness). STRONG LITERARY OBSERVATION.

lines.translit: alka — Adapa — ammīni la takkala la tašatti? — la baltāta?
notes: 'Come — Adapa — why did you not eat, did you not drink? — Are you not (now to be) alive (= immortal)?' Anu's confrontation: he confirms the food/water was of LIFE.

lines.translit: Ea bēlī aqbâ — la takkala la tašatti
notes: 'My lord Ea told me — do not eat, do not drink.' Adapa names Ea as the source of his warning.
'Take him — return him to his earth.' Anu sends Adapa back to mortality.

notes: Fragmentary. The closing of B is uncertain; Foster 2005 supplies a brief restoration based on parallel-text logic.

segments.label: Fragment C — Late Babylonian (small fragment, partial parallel to Fragment B)

preceding_lacuna.text: Fragment C is small and very fragmentary; only the sense of a few lines can be reconstructed.

i18n.en: [Fragment C is small and mostly broken. Only partial readings, including a parallel to part of Fragment B's narrative.]

notes: Fragment C lines are too broken for confident reconstruction. Izre'el 2001 gives a tentative reading. WoH conservative: mark as broken pending verification.

segments.label: Fragment D — Late Babylonian (preserves the catchline)

preceding_lacuna.text: Fragment D is small; its primary value is the surviving catchline.

i18n.en: [Fragment D is small but preserves the catchline (the formula identifying the next composition in the series).]

notes: Fragment D's catchline value is documented in Lambert 1976 and Izre'el 2001. WoH conservative: mark as pending verification.
